report:
**Conclusion:** Your claim is supported, most directly for the specific comparison of *chlorhexidine–alcohol versus iodine–alcohol*. In a large randomized trial (1,147 cesarean deliveries), 30-day surgical-site infection (SSI) occurred in 4.0% with chlorhexidine–alcohol versus 7.3% with iodine–alcohol (risk ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.34–0.90; *P*=0.02). That is a 3.3-percentage-point absolute reduction (about one fewer SSI per 30 preparations). Skin reactions were similar.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048

The cesarean-specific 2018 systematic review/meta-analysis also concluded chlorhexidine–alcohol reduced SSI compared with povidone–iodine preparations, though the evidence base was relatively small and included differing iodine formulations—not always iodine *with alcohol*.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/

**Why not call it settled?** Another randomized cesarean study found very similar SSI rates—4.5% chlorhexidine–alcohol, 4.6% povidone–iodine, and 3.9% sequential preparation (*P*=.85)—but its iodine comparison was not the same iodine–alcohol regimen as the pivotal trial.  
https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/abstract/10.1097/aog.0000000000001118~skin-preparation-for-prevention-of-surgical-site-infection?redirectionsource=fulltextview

A 2024 network meta-analysis ranked alcohol-based 2% chlorhexidine most likely to prevent SSI, but overlapping credible intervals mean it could not establish a statistically clear advantage over all alternatives.  
https://www.journalofhospitalinfection.com/article/S0195-6701(24)00128-2/abstract

So: chlorhexidine–alcohol is a reasonable evidence-based preferred preparation, especially versus iodine–alcohol, but effect size and certainty may vary by formulation, protocol, and setting.
